query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) designed with coherent nanoprecipitates can reduce molten aluminum erosion during the hot dip plating process compared to conventional materials.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional dipping and plating equipment parts (e.g., rollers and guide plates) are typically made from standard alloys or steels that suffer rapid corrosion when in prolonged contact with high‐temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.intervention: Replace or coat the critical parts of the plating equipment with a tungsten RHEA engineered with stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs).
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature molten aluminum over extended operational times typical of hot dip aluminum plating processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent nanoprecipitates in the tungsten RHEA create an ultrastable microstructure that promotes the formation of a protective oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: The durable oxide scale (potentially including tungsten-based oxides and alloy-specific protective phases) that forms on the alloy surface minimizes direct chemical reaction and penetration by the aluminum melt, thereby lowering the corrosion and erosion rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Equipment parts modified with the tungsten RHEA are predicted to exhibit a lower corrosion rate and longer service life relative to parts manufactured from conventional materials.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (corrosion rate, material loss, and service life) of traditional dipping/plating equipment parts under similar high-temperature aluminum exposure.
generation.boundary: While the tungsten RHEA is expected to show improved resistance, the extent of the improvement may depend on specific process variables (e.g., temperature, aluminum chemistry) and thermal cycling effects that have yet to be fully explored.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance and lifetime extension is uncertain without targeted experimentation; interactions between molten aluminum and the specific tungsten alloy constituents need further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of dipping/plating equipment parts: one set made from the tungsten RHEA with SCCPs and one set from the current standard material. Expose both sets to continuous contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum under controlled laboratory conditions that simulate industrial operation. Periodically measure corrosion rates, oxide layer integrity, and mechanical performance over an extended period.
measurements: Weight change and thickness loss of the parts (corrosion rate)
Microstructural analysis (oxide layer formation and integrity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten RHEA parts do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., lower corrosion rate and higher structural integrity) over the conventional parts under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering
